pdf.title: Delayed observations in a finite loss table

sections.heading: Abstract and setup
sections.body:
Suppose a dispatch learner chooses one of two bins before the delayed inspection of the preceding item arrives. The quantity we wish to estimate is the average loss of a fixed bin across a finite stream of T items. It is easy to confuse this target with the loss averaged only over observed items. This note isolates the correction for random delayed observation when the observation rate depends on the bin. The experiments are an illustrative simulation with explicitly generated losses; they do not describe measured deployments.

Index items by t and denote the loss table by l(t,a) in [0,1]. Before each choice the learner knows H(t-1), the sigma-field generated by its previous actions and the inspections that have arrived. The full current loss vector is fixed before the learner draws its action. Conditional on H(t-1), action a is selected with probability q(t,a), bounded below by epsilon. Given a selection, a separate Bernoulli audit coin with success probability s(a) determines whether the loss eventually arrives. The audit coin is independent of the current loss conditional on action and history.

sections.heading: Equation 1 · An identity with a denominator
sections.body:
Define X(t,a)=I(A(t)=a) I(audited) l(t,a)/(q(t,a) s(a)). For a fixed action, conditional expectation over the action draw and the audit coin yields the full table entry. The cancellation works conditionally even though q depends on earlier returned inspections. It fails if one conditions on the realized action too early and silently takes its indicator outside the expectation. The learning rule used after a return is otherwise irrelevant here.

There is a separate question about how the simulator is stopped. If the measurement ends before pending audits have arrived, dropping unresolved items changes the target again. In all tables below we drain the audit queue after selecting the final item. An audit observed during drain retains the index of its original decision.

sections.heading: Experiment 1 · Queue drained vs cut off
sections.body: We generated 12,000 independent two-bin tables per random seed. We compare three reporting routines fed the same decisions, losses and audits. The first routine divides by the number of returned inspections; the second uses inverse propensity weights but ends the run with the action stream; the last both reweights and drains. The table gives mean estimates over 24 seeds. The final column reports a typical queue size immediately after the last decision.

sections.heading: Experiment 2 · Ablation and reading questions
sections.body: For the ablation we halve s(V) while fixing the action floor and the delay distribution. The full estimator still agrees with the fixed-table loss on average, although spread across seeds increases. An unexpectedly small standard error can indicate an experiment that independently redraws losses for each estimator. Write down which parts of the random stream should be shared when comparing the three routines. For a figures-only discussion, explain which comparison isolates the stopping rule and one limitation of extrapolating the finite-stream result.

sections.heading: Appendix A · Second moment and partial identification
sections.body: Start with a single fixed loss entry and compute E[X(t,a)^2 | H(t-1)] by explicitly summing over the event that both indicators equal one. Then upper-bound the conditional variance using l(t,a) <= 1 and q(t,a) >= epsilon. Express the dependence on s(a). Next assume the logging service reports only a range for s(a) rather than its exact value. Determine which steps of the expectation calculation continue to hold and bound the possible bias if an analyst substitutes the midpoint of the range.

sections.heading: Appendix B · What to bring to the board
sections.body:
For the proof track, derive the variance bound and construct a two-item execution in which discarding an unresolved inspection gives a biased report even with correct propensities. Specify the losses, selection probabilities and the audit that arrives late. Show the calculation including the term that disappears if the queue is dropped. Explain whether extending the measurement by a fixed grace period is sufficient when delay has unbounded support.

For the empirical track, read through the experiment section and prepare one slide with a finding, its control and a plausible confound. The appendix derivations are outside that assignment. For either track, do not treat the toy numbers here as measurements of a real system.
